nameStory: Mountain Ricegrass gets its name from its small, rice-like seeds that were historically gathered by Native Americans as a food source. The 'mountain' part refers to its preference for rocky, elevated terrain where it thrives in harsh conditions that would challenge other grasses.
description: Mountain Ricegrass is a hardy perennial bunch grass that forms dense, spiky tufts reaching 1-3 feet tall. Its narrow, rolled leaves give it an almost needle-like appearance, creating tight clumps that look a bit like green pincushions. This tough grass produces delicate, open seed heads in late spring that dance gracefully in mountain breezes. It's built to survive in some of New England's harshest rocky outcrops and exposed ledges.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow leaves that roll inward so tightly they feel almost round when you gently roll them between your fingers - like thin green needles that are surprisingly flexible

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spiky bunches or tufts that feel stiff and bristly to the touch, growing in tight clumps rather than spreading like lawn grass

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces loose, open seed heads on thin stems that nod gracefully in the wind, with small purplish or bronze-tinted spikelets that catch the light

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, rice-like seeds with a distinctive twisted, bent awn (bristle) that looks like a tiny elbow sticking out from each seed

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant feels rough and wiry to the touch, with leaves that make a subtle scratching sound when brushed against

habitat: Look for Mountain Ricegrass on rocky outcrops, cliff faces, and exposed ledges throughout New England's mountains and hills. It thrives in thin, well-drained soils where few other plants can survive, often growing directly from cracks in granite or other bedrock. You'll typically find it on south-facing slopes and ridgetops where the conditions are dry and harsh.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as tight bundles of rolled leaves, and flowering begins in late spring with delicate seed heads appearing on slender stalks.
seasonality.summer: Seeds ripen and the characteristic bent awns become most visible, while the plant maintains its spiky, tufted appearance throughout the hot months.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may take on bronze or purplish tints, and mature seed heads persist, often rattling gently in autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: The tough, wiry leaves remain visible above snow, appearing as stiff, bleached tufts that help identify the plant even in harsh conditions.

funFact: Mountain Ricegrass can live for decades in the same rocky crevice, with some clumps estimated to be over 50 years old - making them among the longest-lived individual grass plants in New England!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other bunch grasses, but Mountain Ricegrass's tightly rolled, needle-like leaves and preference for rocky habitats set it apart. Remember: if it feels like you're touching a spiky pincushion growing from bare rock, you've likely found Mountain Ricegrass.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'ricegrass,' this species isn't closely related to true rice and belongs to a different grass subfamily entirely. The name simply refers to the rice-like appearance of the seeds, which were an important traditional food source.
compareHints: Mountain Ricegrass differs from its relative Canadian Ricegrass by preferring much rockier, more exposed sites rather than woodland edges. Mountain Ricegrass also has more tightly rolled leaves and tends to form denser, more compact tufts. Canadian Ricegrass grows taller and has slightly broader leaves that don't roll as tightly.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canadian Ricegrass differs from its close relative Mountain Ricegrass by preferring rich, moist woodland soils rather than dry, rocky mountain slopes.
